summary: Specifies a combination of the secure RTP profile (SAVP) and the feedback profile (AVPF), allowing secure real-time communication with timely receiver feedback. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: This lets a video call have both a secret code scrambler and a way for the receiver to quickly tell the sender what went wrong.

questions: can secure and insecure rtp profiles be mixed
how is savpf negotiated in sdp
subtitle: A combined RTP profile that gives encrypted, authenticated media sessions the fast receiver feedback of AVPF.

tldr.problem: Secure RTP (SAVP) and the RTCP feedback profile (AVPF) are separate RTP profiles, and only one profile can be negotiated for an RTP session. A session could be secure or get timely feedback, but not both.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5124 defines SAVPF, which layers AVPF on top of SAVP. Both keep their own rules, with a few adjustments such as accounting for the SRTCP overhead in the RTCP size estimate, and SDP gets a new RTP/SAVPF profile name.
tldr.outcome: Secure sessions can now use immediate receiver feedback. SAVPF adds no security services beyond SAVP and takes none away.

today: RFC 5124 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2008. The metadata for this site lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Two Profiles That Could Not Be Combined
sections.content:
RTP carries time-based media across IP, and RTCP lets receivers report on quality. Secure RTP (RFC 3711) defines the SAVP profile for encryption, integrity and replay protection. The extended feedback profile (RFC 4585) defines AVPF, which lets participants give immediate feedback while keeping the average RTCP data rate.

Both are RTP profiles and must be negotiated, usually out-of-band with SDP. A single SDP session-level description cannot negotiate both, so a session had to choose one or the other. RFC 5124 specifies a new profile, SAVPF, that combines them. Because SAVP and AVPF are largely orthogonal, no sophisticated algorithms are needed: the RFC refers to the two profiles and describes only the implications of combining them and the negotiation.
sections.plainLanguage: There were two separate switches for a call, one for secret codes and one for quick feedback, and you could only flip one. This RFC makes a third switch that turns on both.

sections.title: How the Two Layers Fit Together
sections.content:
SAVP sits between RTP and the transport layer, usually UDP, giving a two-layer hierarchy. In SAVPF the upper AVP layer is replaced by AVPF. AVPF changes the timing rules for RTCP and adds feedback packet formats, and that works the same whether or not RTCP is then encrypted or integrity protected. The SAVP part still adds trailing fields to RTP and RTCP packets and applies its cryptographic transforms, unchanged.

The SRTP part acts only when AVPF has scheduled a packet or one arrives from the transport. All RTCP packets MUST be encapsulated as defined in Section 3.4 of RFC 3711, and the AVPF feedback packet formats and extensions MAY be used. The RTCP encryption prefix from RFC 3550 MUST NOT be used in SAVPF.
sections.plainLanguage: Quick feedback decides when to send a note, and the secret code layer wraps each note before it goes out. The two jobs do not get in each other's way.

sections.title: The Cost of Security on Feedback Timing
sections.content:
How often receivers may send feedback depends on the RTCP bandwidth, the group size and the average RTCP packet size. SRTCP adds fields at the end of each RTCP packet, probably at least some 10 to 20 bytes (14 bytes by default), and extensions or longer field lengths MAY add more.

A larger average packet means feedback can be sent less often. Application designers must take precautions to keep the RTCP bandwidth shares, and the RFC says this MUST be done by adjusting the RTCP variable avg_rtcp_size to reflect the size of SRTCP packets.
sections.plainLanguage: A sealed envelope is heavier than a postcard, so you can mail fewer of them in the same time. The sender has to count the envelope's weight when deciding how often to write.

sections.title: Negotiating the Profile in SDP
sections.content:
In SDP the combined profile is called SAVPF, next to AVP, AVPF and SAVP. The SDP attributes for key management (RFC 4567, RFC 4568) and for feedback (RFC 4585) MAY also be used with SAVPF.

In the offer/answer model (RFC 3264), negotiation is per media session. AVP, AVPF, SAVP and SAVPF are mutually exclusive for one media description. An offerer that supports several profiles SHOULD offer all acceptable ones in order of preference and prefer secure over non-secure, but SHOULD NOT mix secure and insecure alternatives in the same offer, which could allow bidding-down attacks. If both are offered, the signaling MUST be protected. The answerer SHOULD prefer a secure profile and otherwise take the first acceptable alternative. If an offer uses SAVPF and the answerer does not support it, the media session MUST be rejected, and an answerer that wants SAVPF when the offer does not use it MUST reject and MAY counter-offer.

With RTSP, the client MUST pick exactly one profile per media stream in the SETUP request, via the Transport header, and the server confirms or refuses. When secure profiles are used, the KeyMgmt header MUST be included. For announcements without negotiation, such as SAP, the initiator SHOULD provide alternative descriptions and SHOULD NOT announce AVP or AVPF sessions unless other security means are used.
sections.plainLanguage: Before a call starts, each side says which kind of call it can do and they agree on one. If one side insists on the secure-with-feedback kind and the other cannot do it, that part of the call is turned down.

sections.title: Mixing Profiles in One Session
sections.content:
SAVP and SAVPF use SRTP, while AVP and AVPF use plain RTP, so the secure and plain groups are not meant to interoperate. AVP and AVPF on one side and SAVP and SAVPF on the other MUST NOT be mixed in the same RTP session.

SAVP and SAVPF entities MAY be mixed in a single RTP session, and so MAY AVP and AVPF entities, following the interworking considerations in Section 5 of RFC 4585. Different RTP sessions can use different profiles arbitrarily.
sections.plainLanguage: Kids who speak in secret code and kids who speak plainly cannot share one conversation. But the kids who use the quick-feedback code and those who do not can still talk together.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
SAVPF inherits its security properties from SAVP and neither adds nor removes security services, so the considerations of RFC 3711 apply. Applying SAVPF implies mandatory integrity protection on RTCP, which blocks false packets from non-members but does not stop a malicious member.

Security SHOULD NOT be traded for interoperability. For confidential or integrity-protected groups the RFC RECOMMENDS not offering alternatives other than SAVP and SAVPF, unless other mechanisms are in place. Master keys follow the RFC 3711 rules: a master key MUST NOT be shared among RTP sessions unless the SSRCs are unique across all their streams. After 2^48 SRTP packets or 2^31 SRTCP packets secured with one key, whichever comes first, key management MUST supply new keys or the session MUST end. Mixing secure and insecure media sessions MUST follow local security policy.

IANA registration: the SDP "proto" value RTP/SAVPF, long form "Secure RTP Profile with RTCP-based Feedback". All attributes defined for RTP/SAVP and RTP/AVPF are valid for it.
sections.plainLanguage: The secret code is as strong as before, no better and no worse. Keys must not be reused forever, and you should not offer a plain version just to be friendly.
